chunks: From him, from Muhammad and Ahmad, the sons of al-Hasan, from their father, from Thalabah ibn Maymun, from Ma'mar ibn Yahya ibn Bassam, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about what people narrate from the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) regarding certain matters of the private parts, which he did not command for others nor forbid for others, except for himself and his offspring. So we said, 'How can that be?' He said, 'A verse made it permissible, and another verse made it forbidden.'

We said, 'Do the two verses mean that one abrogated the other, or are they both clear rulings that should be acted upon together?' He said, 'He has made it clear to them when he forbade it for himself and his offspring.'

We said, 'What prevented him from making that clear to the people?' He said, 'He feared that they would not obey. So if the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) had been firmly established, he would have implemented the entire Book of Allah and all the truth.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali keep certain permissible acts specific to himself and his family according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the concept of *al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh* (abrogation) and *al-Muhkam* (clear/unabrogated) verses, specifically addressing the legal status of *al-Furuj* (sexual relations), often linked to temporary marriage (*Mut'ah*) or specific prohibitions. Imam al-Baqir (AS) explains that while the verses were clear, Ali (AS) restricted the ruling to himself and his progeny to prevent societal disobedience (*Khawf an la yuta'a*) had he made it universally binding, highlighting the pragmatic wisdom of the Imams in applying divine law. This underscores the Shia view that the Imams possess the authority to clarify and implement rulings in a manner that ensures compliance and preserves the integrity of the Sharia.
